author: knoshua
content: I understand this channel is meant for technical discussion. I believe this question qualifies but feel free to let me know if it doesnt. The specification implements the issuance change by adding a `process_issuance_burn` after `process_rewards_and_penalties` instead of  directly reducing rewards and increasing penalties as described by Anders (<https://ethresear.ch/t/properties-of-issuance-offsets-and-increased-penalties-under-low-zero-negative-issuance-policies/25292>). As far as I can tell, this leads to the same end result and I'm wondering if there is a technical reason to prefer one over the other.

author: greystroke
content:
I am not in the issuance should not be touched again camp. I actually think we will need to adjust issuance in order to incentivize a credibly neutral zkprover set as part of the lean ethereum roadmap. 

However, I think changes to the issuance curve need to be much less dramatic (eg. issuance curve should never hit 0%) and needs to first be preceeded by mitigating eips to offset the centralizing pressure an issuance reduction will likely cause (mev burn, encrypted mempools, correlation penalities, etc).

I do think though the next time should be the final time we commit as a community to touch issuance. Otherwise, it will undermine ETH's SoV narrative from which much of its investment value is derived.

author: jasper.the.friendly.ghost
content:
The ACD call and forum post spend a considerable amount of time discussing dilution adjusted yields. I believe an over emphasis on this will lead to incorrect assumption about node operator behavior causing a dramatic fall in the number of home stakers on Ethereum. 


There are currently substantial costs associated with node operation. It’s well established that bandwidth and storage requirements have increased in lock step over the years. Most new node operators have to actively buy a separate new PC (the ideal security practice, anyways) for their node. This runs anywhere from $800-$1500. On top of hardware, individuals often have to upgrade their Internet (shout out Ben Edington among many others) so that they can run their nodes. Some years ago, vitalik wrote an essay in which he used 0.8% per year as a cost for running the node with a single validator (this is justified - the average Rocket Pool node has a single minipool). The exact value doesn’t really matter - what matters is that there’s some cost associated with running a node that is a hurdle to overcome. 

You can only recoup or pay expenses with nominal yield. If ETH deflates 5% but the nominal yield is only 0.001%, your supply adjusted yield is a wonderful 5% with a rounding error. The fact of the matter is that positive issuance is the only incentive we can offer to someone to run a node. 

Any curve that has a 0 intercept will create a race to the bottom of reservation yields. Home node operators have fixed costs - coinbase and co barely do. They are more than happy to stake their customers ETH for them at 0.5% or at 0.01%. They get that customer into their ecosystem and earn most of their money off their trading fees and order flow. In the game of reservation yields, CEXs always win. 

I cannot support any curve that intercepts 0% yield.
